lesson.title: Reading a Species' Story of Life and Death
lesson.summary: A survivorship curve plots the proportion of a cohort still alive at each age, and the shape of that curve, typically classified as Type I, II, or III, summarizes when in life a species faces its greatest risk of dying.
lesson.body:
Population ecology tracks how many individuals are in a population and how that number changes, but it can also zoom in on a single group of same aged individuals, called a cohort, and ask a more specific question: at what point in their lives are members of this cohort most likely to die? A survivorship curve answers that question graphically, by plotting the number or proportion of a cohort's original members that are still alive at each successive age, usually on a graph where the vertical axis uses a logarithmic scale so differences at low survivor numbers remain visible. Reading and comparing these curves is itself a good exercise in data interpretation, since the shape of the line, not just its endpoints, is what carries the biological meaning.

Ecologists generally describe three idealized patterns. A Type I curve stays high and relatively flat through early and middle life, then drops steeply at older ages, meaning most individuals survive childhood and adulthood and death is concentrated later in life. Humans in societies with modern medicine and sanitation, along with elephants, are commonly used examples: most individuals survive to old age, and mortality is heavily weighted toward the final portion of the lifespan. It is worth noting that this is not a fixed property of the species itself so much as a reflection of current conditions. Historically, and in populations without access to modern medical care, human survivorship has looked considerably less like a clean Type I curve, with meaningfully higher mortality in infancy and childhood.

A Type II curve is roughly a straight diagonal line on that log scale, meaning the risk of dying is approximately constant at every age, an individual is about as likely to die in a given time period whether it is young, middle aged, or old. Many bird species, and some rodents and lizards, are commonly cited as approximating this pattern, since predation and other risks that do not particularly discriminate by age can dominate their mortality.

A Type III curve is the mirror image of Type I: extremely high mortality very early in life, followed by a marked leveling off for the relative few individuals that survive that initial gauntlet. Oysters are a classic example, along with many fish, most insects, and many plants: a single female oyster can release enormous numbers of larvae, the overwhelming majority of which die within days as plankton or newly settled juveniles, but those rare individuals that make it past that vulnerable stage then have comparatively good odds of surviving much longer.

These three shapes are useful reference points, but real species often fall somewhere between them or shift depending on environmental conditions, so they are best treated as a framework for organizing observations rather than a rigid classification every species must fit into cleanly. As the next chapter explores, the shape of a species' survivorship curve is closely tied to its broader life history strategy, since how likely an individual is to die at a given age shapes how natural selection favors it to allocate energy toward growth, survival, and reproduction.
